minor_characters.name: Owl Eyes
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Turns up in Gatsby’s library at the first big party (003), is present at the roadside car wreck that night (003), and reappears at the graveside in the published text (009).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He supplies comic color and a redundant witness perspective; his functions can be absorbed into narration, and the synopsis’s funeral headcount excludes him.

minor_characters.name: Ewing Klipspringer
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Gatsby’s quasi-boarder who plays the piano during the reunion (005) and later phones about his tennis shoes instead of attending the funeral (009).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He merely underlines fair‑weather friendships, which the abridgment can state directly without a named character.

minor_characters.name: Catherine
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Myrtle Wilson’s sister who attends the New York apartment party (002) and later appears at the inquest (009).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her gossip and later evasions do not affect the affair, the crash, or Wilson’s actions.

minor_characters.name: Chester McKee
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A vapid photographer from downstairs who joins the apartment gathering (002).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He is pure satire of the party’s milieu and has no bearing on plot or themes that aren’t conveyed elsewhere.

minor_characters.name: Mrs. McKee
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Chester’s wife, another guest at Myrtle’s apartment party (002).
minor_characters.reason_removable: She adds only background chatter and can be cut with no story consequence.

minor_characters.name: Mr. Sloane
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Arrives on horseback with Tom and a lady to Gatsby’s mansion and offers a faux dinner invitation (006).
minor_characters.reason_removable: This social skirmish can go without changing Tom’s later confrontation with Gatsby or Daisy’s reaction to West Egg.

minor_characters.name: Lucille
minor_characters.appearances_summary: One of the ‘girls in yellow’ at Gatsby’s party who tells the torn‑dress anecdote (003).
minor_characters.reason_removable: She is party color only and does not recur or affect events.

minor_characters.name: Ferdie
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Daisy’s chauffeur briefly named when she arrives for tea at Nick’s cottage (005).
minor_characters.reason_removable: A one‑line functionary whose mention can be dropped without loss.

minor_characters.name: Slagle
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Calls Nick from Chicago after Gatsby’s death about a botched bond scheme involving ‘Young Parke’ (009).
minor_characters.reason_removable: This stray criminal thread is extraneous once Tom exposes Gatsby’s dealings and Gatsby is dead.

minor_characters.name: Stella
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Wolfshiem’s office assistant who stonewalls Nick before Wolfshiem refuses the funeral (009).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her comic business can be summarized in a sentence about Wolfshiem declining to come.

minor_characters.name: Walter Chase
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A name Tom drops at the Plaza to smear Gatsby with bootlegging specifics (007).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Tom’s point—that Gatsby’s money is illicit—lands without this extra proper noun.

minor_characters.name: Pammy Buchanan
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Daisy and Tom’s young daughter who appears once at the luncheon before the drive to town (007).
minor_characters.reason_removable: Her brief cameo can be omitted without altering the triangle, the confrontation, or Daisy’s characterization in the synopsis.

minor_characters.name: Benny McClenahan
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A recurrent name on Nick’s catalog of Gatsby’s party guests, always arriving with ‘four girls’ (004).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He exists only inside a guest‑list catalog that can be cut.

minor_characters.name: Doctor Webster Civet
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A party acquaintance mentioned at Gatsby’s gathering (003) and on the guest‑list roll (004).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He’s incidental and contributes nothing to the main arc.

minor_characters.name: Rosy Rosenthal
minor_characters.appearances_summary: A murdered gangster in Wolfshiem’s Metropole anecdote (004).
minor_characters.reason_removable: He’s used only to shade Wolfshiem; if that anecdote goes, so can he.

minor_characters.name: Mrs. Sigourney Howard
minor_characters.appearances_summary: Jordan Baker’s aunt, name‑checked as her chaperone/phone‑book listing (003–004).
minor_characters.reason_removable: A throwaway reference that doesn’t affect Jordan’s role or Nick’s relationship.

subplots.name: Nick’s office routines and brief Jersey City romance
subplots.reason_removable: These personal asides don’t influence the Gatsby–Daisy–Tom arc or Nick’s final disillusionment, which the synopsis already covers.

subplots.name: Owl Eyes’ post‑party car wreck
subplots.reason_removable: A comic detour that neither advances the plot nor changes anyone’s choices.

subplots.name: Gatsby’s ‘white card’ that gets him waved past a traffic cop
subplots.reason_removable: A throwaway episode that adds flash but no necessary information about his crimes or character beyond what the confrontation supplies.

subplots.name: Mr. Sloane’s horseback drop‑in and faux dinner invitation
subplots.reason_removable: This social skirmish is easily excised while keeping Tom’s subsequent attendance at Gatsby’s party and the rising rivalry.

subplots.name: Myrtle’s spur‑of‑the‑moment puppy purchase
subplots.reason_removable: A comic detail that does not affect the affair, the apartment party, or the fatal chain of events.

subplots.name: Michaelis’s overnight vigil and the hour‑by‑hour map of Wilson’s movements
subplots.reason_removable: The novel can state succinctly that the grief‑crazed Wilson, misled about the driver and lover, tracks Gatsby and kills him.

subplots.name: Chicago phone call about ‘Young Parke’ after Gatsby’s death
subplots.reason_removable: This dangling crime subplot adds atmosphere but no outcome the synopsis requires.

subplots.name: Pammy’s presentation at the Buchanan house
subplots.reason_removable: Her cameo can be lifted without changing the confrontation in the Plaza, the hit‑and‑run, or Daisy and Tom’s later flight.

subplots.name: Jordan Baker’s old golf‑cheating scandal and Nick’s Warwick anecdote
subplots.reason_removable: Nick’s breakup with Jordan can rest on his broader disgust without reprising this separate sports scandal.

digressions.topic: Nick’s roll‑call catalog of Gatsby’s summer guests (‘timetable’ of names)
digressions.reason_removable: A long social taxonomy that adds texture only and can be cut without affecting events or core themes.

digressions.topic: Oranges, juicers, caterers, and orchestra inventories that itemize Gatsby’s parties
digressions.reason_removable: Lavish logistics can be condensed to a line or two while preserving the idea of nightly extravagance.

digressions.topic: Wolfshiem’s Metropole reminiscence about Rosy Rosenthal’s murder
digressions.reason_removable: An anecdotal sidebar that isn’t needed once Wolfshiem’s identity as a fixer/gambler is established.

digressions.topic: Nick’s Manhattan twilight vignettes imagining affairs with passing strangers
digressions.reason_removable: An essayistic mood piece that can be trimmed without changing any decisions or relationships.

digressions.topic: The meandering ‘Biloxi’ wedding‑day anecdote during the Plaza showdown
digressions.reason_removable: A comic detour that interrupts the confrontation without altering its outcome.

digressions.topic: Nick’s extended Midwestern homecoming reverie (Union Station, holiday trains, El Greco vision of West Egg)
digressions.reason_removable: The return‑to‑the‑Midwest decision and the green‑light meditation can stand without the travelogue and tableau.

digressions.topic: Minute‑by‑minute geography of Wilson’s route (Port Roosevelt, Gad’s Hill) as reconstructed by Michaelis
digressions.reason_removable: Procedural mapping adds little once we state simply that Wilson, believing Gatsby responsible, seeks him out and kills him.
